name: Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand, shoulder-width grip, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps at the top, then lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The classic mass-builder for the biceps — keep the elbows pinned to your sides throughout the entire rep.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides, don't let them drift forward.
Avoid swinging the torso to help lift the weight.
commonMistakes: Using body momentum to swing the bar up.
Letting the elbows travel forward during the curl.
benefits: Simple, effective mass builder for the biceps.
Easy to progressively overload with added plates.
safetyNotes: Use a weight that allows strict elbow position.
Keep the lower back neutral, avoid excessive arching.
startingPosition: Arms fully extended, bar held at the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand holding a barbell with a grip wider than shoulder-width, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The wider grip tends to emphasize the short (inner) head of the biceps more than a standard-width curl.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides throughout.
Avoid letting the wrists bend back under load.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the bar up.
Gripping too wide, which can strain the wrists.
benefits: Shifts emphasis toward the inner biceps head.
Simple grip-width variation to add exercise variety.
safetyNotes: Keep wrists neutral and firm.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, wide overhand-underhand curl grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Close-Grip Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand holding a barbell with a grip narrower than shoulder-width, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The narrower grip tends to place more emphasis on the long (outer) head of the biceps.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked close to the body.
Control the descent rather than dropping the weight.
commonMistakes: Flaring the elbows out to compensate for the narrow grip.
Using too much weight and shortening the range of motion.
benefits: Shifts emphasis toward the outer biceps head.
Good variation to pair with a wide-grip curl for full development.
safetyNotes: Keep wrists neutral throughout.
Avoid excessive weight that causes elbow flare.
startingPosition: Arms extended, narrow grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: EZ Bar Curl
instructions: Stand holding an EZ bar on the angled grips, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar, making it a common substitute for lifters with wrist discomfort.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso to generate momentum.
Only completing a partial range of motion.
benefits: Wrist-friendly alternative to a straight barbell curl.
Still allows heavy progressive overload.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Avoid locking out the elbows aggressively at the bottom.
startingPosition: Arms extended, EZ bar held at the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Standing Dumbbell Curl
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with arms fully extended, palms facing forward.
Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a more natural wrist path and independent arm control compared to a barbell.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides throughout.
Avoid swinging the dumbbells up using the hips.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to heave the weight up.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
benefits: Independent arm control reduces strength imbalances.
Allows a full range of motion and wrist rotation.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Keep the core braced to avoid leaning back.
startingPosition: Arms extended, dumbbells at the sides, palms forward.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up near the shoulders.

name: Seated Dumbbell Curl
instructions: Sit upright on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms fully extended.
Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Sitting removes the ability to use body momentum, keeping the tension strictly on the biceps.
tips: Sit tall and keep the torso still throughout.
Squeeze the biceps at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to help lift the weight.
Rushing through reps without a full contraction.
benefits: Removes momentum for a stricter curl.
Good option when a bench is available for extra stability.
safetyNotes: Keep the back flat against the bench pad.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Seated, arms extended, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up near the shoulders.

name: Alternating Dumbbell Curl
instructions: Stand or sit holding a dumbbell in each hand, arms fully extended.
Curl one dumbbell up toward the shoulder while the other stays extended.
Lower with control, then repeat on the other side, alternating throughout the set.
coachNote: Alternating sides allows a slightly heavier load per arm since you're not lifting both simultaneously.
tips: Keep the resting arm fully extended and still.
Focus on a full squeeze at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes: Swinging the torso side to side to assist the curl.
Rushing between sides instead of controlling each rep.
benefits: Allows focused attention on each arm individually.
Slightly heavier loading potential than simultaneous curls.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced to avoid excessive torso rotation.
Control the descent on both arms.
startingPosition: Arms extended, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: One dumbbell curled up near the shoulder.

name: Hammer Curl
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip, palms facing each other.
Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders, keeping the neutral grip throughout.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The neutral grip shifts emphasis onto the brachialis and brachioradialis, adding thickness to the arm alongside the biceps.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Avoid rotating the wrists during the curl.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
benefits: Builds forearm and brachialis size alongside the biceps.
Wrist-friendly grip for most lifters.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Arms extended, dumbbells at the sides, neutral grip.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up near the shoulders.

name: Cross-Body Hammer Curl
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip.
Curl one dumbbell up and across the body toward the opposite shoulder.
Lower with control, then repeat on the other side, alternating throughout the set.
coachNote: The diagonal path targets the brachialis slightly differently than a standard hammer curl.
tips: Keep the elbow relatively fixed as the forearm crosses the body.
Avoid rotating the torso to assist the curl.
commonMistakes: Swinging the body to help lift the weight.
Curling straight up instead of across the body.
benefits: Adds variety to standard hammer curl training.
Continues to build forearm and brachialis thickness.
safetyNotes: Keep the core braced to avoid excessive rotation.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, dumbbells at the sides, neutral grip.
endingPosition: Dumbbell curled up and across toward the opposite shoulder.

name: Rope Hammer Curl (Cable)
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a rope attachment with a neutral grip.
Curl the rope up toward your shoulders, keeping the neutral grip.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cable tension stays constant throughout, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the top of the curl.
tips: Keep the elbows pinned to your sides.
Squeeze the rope ends apart slightly at the top for extra contraction.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to help move the weight.
Letting the elbows drift forward during the curl.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Builds brachialis and forearm thickness.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, rope held with a neutral grip.
endingPosition: Rope curled up near the shoulders.

name: Concentration Curl
instructions: Sit on a bench with legs spread, bracing the working elbow against the inner thigh.
Curl the dumbbell up toward the shoulder.
Lower with control back to a full arm extension.
coachNote: Bracing the elbow against the thigh eliminates any momentum, making this one of the strictest biceps isolation exercises.
tips: Keep the elbow fixed against the thigh throughout.
Focus on a strong peak contraction at the top.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift off the thigh.
Using a weight too heavy to control strictly.
benefits: Excellent for mind-muscle connection.
Isolates the biceps without any assistance from momentum.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate weight to maintain strict form.
Keep the wrist neutral throughout.
startingPosition: Seated, elbow braced against the inner thigh, arm extended.
endingPosition: Dumbbell curled up near the shoulder.

name: Barbell Preacher Curl
instructions: Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting flat against the pad, holding an EZ bar.
Lower the bar until your arms are nearly fully extended.
Curl the bar back up toward the shoulders, then repeat.
coachNote: The preacher pad prevents any elbow drift or momentum, isolating the biceps very strictly.
tips: Don't fully lock out the elbows at the bottom to keep tension on the biceps.
Keep the upper arms glued to the pad throughout.
commonMistakes: Lifting the elbows off the pad to cheat the weight up.
Using excessive weight and bouncing out of the bottom position.
benefits: Removes momentum for very strict biceps isolation.
Strong stretch-focused position at the bottom.
safetyNotes: Avoid fully locking out at the bottom under heavy load.
Use a controlled tempo throughout.
startingPosition: Upper arms on the preacher pad, arms nearly extended.
endingPosition: Bar curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Dumbbell Preacher Curl
instructions: Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting against the pad, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Lower the dumbbells until your arms are nearly fully extended.
Curl back up toward the shoulders.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow independent arm control on the preacher bench, useful for correcting side-to-side imbalances.
tips: Keep the upper arms glued to the pad throughout.
Avoid fully locking out the elbows under load.
commonMistakes: Lifting the elbows off the pad.
Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Strong stretch-focused isolation for the biceps.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Avoid excessive weight that forces cheating.
startingPosition: Upper arms on the preacher pad, arms nearly extended.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Machine Preacher Curl
instructions: Sit in the preacher curl machine with your upper arms against the pad, gripping the handles.
Curl the handles up toward the shoulders.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A great beginner-friendly isolation option since the machine controls the movement path for you.
tips: Adjust the seat so your armpits rest at the top of the pad.
Focus on a slow, controlled tempo.
commonMistakes: Seat set too high or low, changing the pressing angle unintentionally.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Very beginner-friendly with a fixed, safe path.
Good biceps isolation without stabilizer demand.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat height correctly before loading.
Avoid locking out aggressively at the bottom.
startingPosition: Upper arms on the pad, arms extended.
endingPosition: Handles curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Single-Arm Preacher Curl (Dumbbell)
instructions: Sit at the preacher bench with one arm resting against the pad, holding a dumbbell.
Lower the dumbbell until the arm is nearly fully extended.
Curl back up toward the shoulder, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time on the preacher bench allows a stronger mind-muscle connection and helps correct imbalances.
tips: Keep the upper arm glued to the pad throughout.
Focus on a full stretch at the bottom of each rep.
commonMistakes: Lifting the elbow off the pad.
Using the free hand to assist the lift.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Strong stretch and peak contraction combination.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Avoid excessive weight that forces cheating.
startingPosition: Upper arm on the preacher pad, arm nearly extended.
endingPosition: Dumbbell curled up toward the shoulder.

name: EZ Bar Spider Curl
instructions: Lie face down on an incline bench with arms hanging straight down, holding an EZ bar.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to a full arm extension.
coachNote: The face-down position removes all momentum and shoulder involvement, isolating the biceps very strictly.
tips: Keep the upper arms vertical throughout the movement.
Focus on a strong peak contraction at the top.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward to help lift the weight.
Using a bench angle too shallow to hang the arms freely.
benefits: Extremely strict biceps isolation.
Strong stretch at the bottom of the movement.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Avoid excessive weight that forces upper body movement.
startingPosition: Face down on incline bench, arms hanging straight down.
endingPosition: Bar curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Dumbbell Spider Curl
instructions: Lie face down on an incline bench with arms hanging straight down, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to a full arm extension.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a slight wrist rotation at the top for an added peak contraction compared to a fixed bar.
tips: Keep the upper arms vertical throughout.
Rotate the wrists slightly outward at the top for extra contraction.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward.
Using too much weight and losing the strict path.
benefits: Extremely strict biceps isolation.
Allows independent arm control and wrist rotation.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Keep the bench angle steep enough for arms to hang freely.
startingPosition: Face down on incline bench, arms hanging straight down.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
instructions: Sit back on an incline bench with arms hanging straight down, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to a full stretch.
coachNote: The incline position puts the biceps in a lengthened position at the bottom, creating a strong stretch stimulus.
tips: Keep the upper arms behind the torso line throughout.
Avoid letting the shoulders roll forward to cheat the weight up.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up.
Letting the elbows drift forward, reducing the stretch.
benefits: Strong stretch-focused position for hypertrophy.
Removes the ability to use body momentum.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Keep the shoulders pinned back against the bench.
startingPosition: Seated on incline bench, arms hanging straight down.
endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up near the shoulders.

name: Barbell Drag Curl
instructions: Stand holding a barbell with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Curl the bar up while dragging it along your torso, pulling the elbows back as you go.
Lower with control back to the starting position, keeping the bar close to the body.
coachNote: Dragging the bar up the torso keeps the shoulders out of the movement, forcing the biceps to do all the work.
tips: Keep the bar in constant contact with the torso.
Pull the elbows back and behind the torso line as you curl.
commonMistakes: Letting the bar drift away from the body, turning it into a standard curl.
Using the shoulders to help lift the weight.
benefits: Removes shoulder involvement for stricter biceps isolation.
Unique variation to break through curling plateaus.
safetyNotes: Use a lighter weight than a standard barbell curl while learning the pattern.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Arms extended, bar held against the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar dragged up the torso to chest height, elbows pulled back.

name: Zottman Curl
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand with an underhand grip, arms extended.
Curl the dumbbells up as in a standard curl, then rotate the wrists so palms face down at the top.
Lower the dumbbells with the palms-down grip, then rotate back to underhand at the bottom.
coachNote: This combines a biceps curl on the way up with a reverse curl on the way down, training both the biceps and forearms in one movement.
tips: Control the descent carefully in the palms-down position — this is where forearm work happens.
Use a lighter weight than your standard curl to manage the rotation.
commonMistakes: Rushing the wrist rotation at the top.
Using too much weight and losing control during the eccentric.
benefits: Trains both biceps and forearm extensors in a single exercise.
Efficient way to combine two training goals in one movement.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo throughout, especially on the lowering phase.
Start light to learn the rotation pattern.
startingPosition: Arms extended, dumbbells at the sides, underhand grip.
endingPosition: Dumbbells lowered with a palms-down grip after the curl and rotation.

name: Barbell Reverse Curl
instructions: Stand holding a barbell with an overhand, shoulder-width grip, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping the overhand grip.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The overhand grip shifts most of the work onto the brachialis and forearm extensors rather than the biceps directly.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Use a lighter weight than your standard curl since grip strength is often the limiting factor.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and losing wrist control.
Swinging the torso to generate momentum.
benefits: Builds forearm and brachialis size.
Improves grip strength alongside arm development.
safetyNotes: Keep wrists as neutral as possible under the overhand grip.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, overhand grip on the bar.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: EZ Bar Reverse Curl
instructions: Stand holding an EZ bar on the angled grips with an overhand grip.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The angled EZ bar grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar reverse curl.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Use a lighter weight than a standard EZ bar curl.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and losing wrist control.
Swinging the torso for momentum.
benefits: Wrist-friendly forearm and brachialis builder.
Good alternative for lifters with wrist discomfort on a straight bar.
safetyNotes: Keep wrists as neutral as the grip allows.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, overhand grip on the EZ bar.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Cable Curl (Straight Bar)
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a straight bar attachment with an underhand grip.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension on the biceps throughout, unlike free weights which can lose tension at the top or bottom.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Avoid leaning back to help move the weight.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the bar up.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Easy to adjust load in small increments.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, bar held with an underhand grip.
endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Cable Rope Curl
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a rope attachment with a neutral, underhand-leaning grip.
Curl the rope up toward your shoulders, twisting the wrists outward slightly at the top.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The rope's free movement allows a slight supination at the top for a stronger peak biceps contraction.
tips: Rotate the wrists outward as you approach the top of the curl.
Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the rope up.
Skipping the wrist rotation at the top.
benefits: Allows a stronger peak contraction than a fixed bar.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arms extended, rope held with a neutral-underhand grip.
endingPosition: Rope curled up near the shoulders, wrists rotated outward.

name: Single-Arm Cable Curl
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a single handle with an underhand grip.
Curl the handle up toward your shoulder.
Lower with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time on the cable allows a strong mind-muscle connection and constant tension throughout.
tips: Keep the elbow fixed at your side.
Avoid rotating the torso to assist the curl.
commonMistakes: Using the free hand to help lift the weight.
Leaning back to generate momentum.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Constant tension throughout the full range.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a controlled tempo.
startingPosition: Arm extended, handle held with an underhand grip.
endingPosition: Handle curled up near the shoulder.

name: High Cable Curl (Double Biceps Pose)
instructions: Stand centered between two high cable pulleys, gripping a handle in each hand with arms out to the sides.
Curl both handles up toward your head, similar to a double biceps bodybuilding pose.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The high pulley angle emphasizes the biceps peak differently than a standard low-to-high curl.
tips: Keep the upper arms roughly parallel to the floor throughout.
Focus on squeezing the biceps hard at the top.
commonMistakes: Dropping the upper arms during the curl, reducing tension.
Using momentum instead of a controlled contraction.
benefits: Unique angle for biceps peak development.
Constant cable tension throughout the range.
safetyNotes: Use a light-to-moderate weight to master the angle.
Keep footing stable throughout.
startingPosition: Arms extended out to the sides at the high pulleys.
endingPosition: Handles curled up toward the head.

name: Cable Preacher Curl
instructions: Position a preacher bench in front of a low cable pulley and rest your upper arms on the pad, gripping a straight bar attachment.
Lower the bar until your arms are nearly fully extended.
Curl back up toward the shoulders.
coachNote: Combining the preacher position with cable tension keeps the biceps under constant load throughout the entire range, unlike a free-weight preacher curl.
tips: Keep the upper arms glued to the pad throughout.
Avoid fully locking out the elbows under load.
commonMistakes: Lifting the elbows off the pad.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Combines strict positioning with constant cable tension.
Strong stretch-focused isolation for the biceps.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled tempo.
Avoid excessive weight that forces cheating.
startingPosition: Upper arms on the preacher pad, arms nearly extended, cable attachment in hand.
endingPosition: Bar curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Overhead Cable Curl
instructions: Stand between two high cable pulleys, or use a single high pulley behind you, gripping a handle with the arm extended overhead-ish behind the body.
Curl the handle toward your head by bending the elbow.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The overhead cable angle puts the long head of the biceps in a stretched position throughout the set, a unique stimulus compared to standard curls.
tips: Keep the upper arm relatively fixed in position.
Focus on a controlled tempo through the stretched range.
commonMistakes: Letting the upper arm drift forward to make the curl easier.
Using too much weight for the stretched position.
benefits: Trains the biceps long head in a lengthened position.
Adds variety for lifters chasing a fuller biceps peak.
safetyNotes: Use light-to-moderate weight to control the stretched position safely.
Keep footing and posture stable throughout.
startingPosition: Arm extended behind and slightly overhead, gripping the handle.
endingPosition: Handle curled toward the head.

name: Behind-the-Back Cable Curl (Bayesian Curl)
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley, arm extended behind the body holding the handle.
Curl the handle forward and up toward the shoulder.
Lower with control back to the starting position behind the body.
coachNote: This popular modern variation stretches the biceps behind the torso, providing tension in a range that standard curls don't reach.
tips: Keep the elbow relatively fixed as you curl forward.
Use a light-to-moderate weight since the stretched position is demanding.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso to assist the curl.
Using too much weight and losing control in the stretched position.
benefits: Provides tension in a stretched position most curls miss.
Popular for maximizing biceps hypertrophy stimulus.
safetyNotes: Start light to learn the unfamiliar positioning.
Keep a stable, braced stance throughout.
startingPosition: Arm extended behind the body, handle in hand.
endingPosition: Handle curled forward and up toward the shoulder.

name: Barbell 21s
instructions: Hold a barbell with an underhand grip, arms fully extended.
Perform 7 curls from the bottom to the midpoint (elbow at 90 degrees).
Perform 7 curls from the midpoint to the top.
Finish with 7 full-range curls from the bottom all the way to the top.
coachNote: A classic biceps burnout technique — use a lighter weight than your normal curl since the partial reps add up to significant total volume.
tips: Keep strict form throughout all three segments.
Reduce the weight if form starts to break down partway through.
commonMistakes: Using a weight too heavy to complete all 21 reps with control.
Rushing through the partial rep ranges.
benefits: High-volume finisher for maximizing biceps fatigue.
Trains the biceps through specific sub-ranges of motion.
safetyNotes: Use a lighter weight than standard curls.
Stop if grip or form breaks down significantly.
startingPosition: Arms extended, bar at the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar curled fully to the shoulders after completing all three segments.

name: Dumbbell Waiter Curl
instructions: Hold a single dumbbell vertically with both hands cupping the top of the handle, like a waiter carrying a tray.
Curl the dumbbell up toward your chin.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The vertical grip emphasizes the long head of the biceps and adds a light peak-contraction stimulus.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Grip the dumbbell securely with both hands throughout.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the weight up.
Letting the dumbbell tilt during the curl.
benefits: Unique grip variation for biceps peak development.
Simple, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate weight to maintain a secure grip.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Dumbbell held vertically at the thighs with both hands.
endingPosition: Dumbbell curled up toward the chin.

name: Plate Curl
instructions: Hold a weight plate with both hands at the edges, arms extended in front of your thighs.
Curl the plate up toward your chest.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A simple accessible option when barbells or dumbbells aren't available — the pinch grip on the plate edges also challenges the forearms.
tips: Grip the plate firmly at the edges.
Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the plate up.
Gripping the plate too loosely, causing it to shift.
benefits: Adds a grip-strength component to a standard curl.
Minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a plate weight you can grip securely.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Plate held at the thighs with both hands.
endingPosition: Plate curled up toward the chest.

name: Kettlebell Curl
instructions: Stand holding a kettlebell in each hand by the handle, arms fully extended.
Curl the kettlebells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The kettlebell's offset weight distribution demands slightly more forearm and grip stabilization than a standard dumbbell curl.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
Grip the handle securely throughout the curl.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the kettlebells up.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
benefits: Builds grip and forearm stability alongside the biceps.
Good option when only kettlebells are available.
safetyNotes: Use a weight you can control through the full range.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Arms extended, kettlebells at the sides.
endingPosition: Kettlebells curled up near the shoulders.

name: Machine Bicep Curl
instructions: Sit in the machine with your upper arms resting on the support, gripping the handles.
Curl the handles up toward the shoulders.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A stable, guided option for beginners or for training close to failure safely.
tips: Adjust the seat so the elbows align with the machine's pivot point.
Focus on a slow, controlled tempo.
commonMistakes: Seat set incorrectly, changing the pivot alignment.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Guided path reduces stabilizer demand.
Easy to progressively overload with the weight stack.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Avoid locking out aggressively at the bottom.
startingPosition: Upper arms supported, arms extended.
endingPosition: Handles curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Resistance Band Curl
instructions: Stand on the middle of a resistance band, holding one end in each hand at your sides.
Curl both hands up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient, joint-friendly option for travel or home biceps training when no weights are available.
tips: Stand wider on the band for more resistance.
Keep the elbows fixed at your sides.
commonMistakes: Using a band too heavy to control with strict form.
Letting the elbows drift forward.
benefits: Portable and joint-friendly.
Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Standing on the band, hands at the sides.
endingPosition: Hands curled up near the shoulders.

name: TRX Bicep Curl
instructions: Hold the TRX handles and lean back with arms extended, body in a straight line, feet planted.
Curl your body up by bending the elbows, bringing your hands toward your forehead.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Difficulty is adjusted by changing your body angle — more upright is easier, more horizontal is harder.
tips: Keep the body rigid like a plank throughout.
Adjust foot position to change difficulty on the fly.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag.
Using a body angle too difficult for current strength level.
benefits: Highly scalable difficulty via body angle.
Portable, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Ensure the TRX anchor point is secure before use.
Keep the core braced throughout.

instructions: Sit back on an incline bench positioned in front of a low cable pulley, holding a handle in each hand.

name: Standing Low Cable Curl
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a handle in each hand, arms extended.
Curl both handles up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control back to the starting position.

Use a controlled tempo.

endingPosition: Handles curled up near the shoulders.

name: Reverse Grip Cable Curl
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a straight bar with an overhand grip.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping the overhand grip.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Combines the forearm and brachialis emphasis of a reverse curl with the constant tension of a cable.

Leaning back to generate momentum.

Use a controlled tempo.

endingPosition: Bar curled up near the shoulders.

name: Dumbbell Hammer Preacher Curl
instructions: Sit at the preacher bench with your upper arms resting on the pad, holding dumbbells with a neutral grip.

Curl back up toward the shoulders, keeping the neutral grip throughout.

Using too much weight and losing strict form.

endingPosition: Dumbbells curled up toward the shoulders.

name: Cable Drag Curl
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a straight bar with an underhand grip.
Curl the bar up while dragging it along your torso, pulling the elbows back as you go.
Lower with control back to the starting position, keeping the bar close to the body.
